analysis.one_liner: Ends employers' tax deductions for anti-union campaigns and requires reporting of that spending.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 118 sponsors including one Republican, but the House Ways and Means Committee never acted on it and it died when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would end a tax break: companies could no longer deduct the cost of campaigns to persuade their own employees against joining or supporting a union. It would also require employers to report that spending to the IRS, including dates, amounts, and disclosures already required under federal labor law. The bill never received a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers deciding whether to organize gain, because employer anti-union campaigns — which the bill's findings say cost companies about $340 million a year on outside consultants alone — would become more expensive and visible. Unions gain a fairer organizing environment. Taxpayers gain modestly because they stop subsidizing employer persuasion campaigns through the deduction.

how_it_helps.text: Denies businesses a tax deduction for spending meant to influence their employees about labor organizations, union elections, labor disputes, or collective action, ending what the bill calls a taxpayer subsidy of employer persuasion campaigns.

Requires employers to report anti-union spending to the IRS at least yearly (up to quarterly), including dates, amounts, whether the activity led to an unfair labor practice complaint or settlement, and copies of disclosures required under the Labor-Management Reporting and Disclosure Act.

Strips the deduction from spending connected to conduct the National Labor Relations Board has charged as an unfair labor practice, or that was settled with the NLRB, unless a court later sets the complaint aside — so illegal union-busting gets no tax write-off.

Carves out ordinary employer functions: bargaining directly with a chosen union representative, communications with shareholders, voluntary union recognition, grievance and labor-management partnership procedures under a contract, legally required postings, and anything a labor union itself pays for.

The bill's findings cite Economic Policy Institute research that roughly 4 in 10 union elections in 2016–2017 involved an unfair labor practice charge against the employer, rising above 54% in larger bargaining units — the conduct the bill targets.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that run anti-union campaigns pay more: the deduction denial raises their taxable income, and the new reporting adds compliance work each quarter. Union-avoidance consultants and related vendors face reduced demand as their clients' after-tax cost of campaigns rises. The conduct itself stays legal; only the subsidy ends.

drawbacks.text: The deduction denial reaches wages paid for producing, conducting, or attending any meeting or training where labor organizations are discussed and bargaining-unit employees attend — language broad enough to sweep in routine managerial meetings and trainings, raising costs beyond targeted union-busting.

Tax treatment would turn on unresolved allegations: the deduction is denied when the NLRB issues a complaint, unless the complaint is later set aside, so employers lose the write-off years before the charge is finally adjudicated.

The bill changes the price of anti-union campaigning, not its legality — a well-funded employer can still run the same campaign and simply absorb the higher after-tax cost, so the measure deters at the margin rather than preventing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a narrow, well-targeted tax change: it extends the existing rule that political lobbying is not deductible to employer campaigns against their own workers' organizing, while explicitly preserving direct bargaining, voluntary recognition, and routine contract administration. The main real costs are compliance — quarterly reporting and the risk that ordinary meetings get caught by the broad meeting-and-training language — and the unfairness of denying a deduction on the basis of an NLRB complaint before final adjudication. Those are manageable design flaws, not reasons the bill fails its purpose.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Donald Norcross introduced the bill on July 20, 2022, with 99 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which holds jurisdiction over the Internal Revenue Code.
Support grew to 117 cosponsors — 116 Democrats and one Republican, Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania — but the action history shows no committee hearing, no markup, and no vote at any point.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and all bills not enacted, including this one, died with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that spend on anti-union campaigns keep the full tax deduction for that spending, and the union-avoidance consultant industry keeps its roughly $340-million-a-year market untouched. Workers gained nothing from the bill's death.

sides.party_line_note: 116 of 213 House Democrats sponsored or cosponsored the bill, joined by exactly one Republican; no vote was ever taken, so the partisan split was never tested on the floor.

industries.note: The bill's findings cite Economic Policy Institute research that companies spend about $340 million a year on outside consultants to sway workers' opinions about unions. Making that spending nondeductible and reportable raises its after-tax cost and exposes it, shrinking the market for these firms.

These employers would pay more out of pocket for captive-audience meetings, surveillance-related campaigns, and consultant work, and would have to report the spending to the IRS quarterly. Their interest in keeping the deduction runs directly against workers' organizing rights.

Union organizing elections would become less lopsided, since employer persuasion campaigns would lose their taxpayer subsidy and face public reporting. Unions' own spending is expressly excluded from the bill's coverage.
